TextBlock.TextLine: Introduction

It
is
not
uncommon
in
the
marine
world
to
find
organisms
living
in
host - guest

relations
with
one
another .
One
such
example
in
the
rocky
intertidal
zone
of
Monterey
Bay

is
the
interaction
between
Crepidula
adunca
( commonly
known
as
the
slipper
snail )
and
its

snail
host ,
Tegula
funebralis
( hereafter
they
will
be
referred
to
as
Crepidula
and
Tegula

respectively ) .
This
study
examined
why
and
how
Crepidula
chose
their
host
snail .

Crepidula
are
sequential
hermaphrodites ,
which
means
they
reproduce
as
one
sex
( in

this
case
males )
early
in
life ,
then
change
to
the
other
sex
for
the
remainder
of
their
life
span

( Hobday
1997 ) .
Crepidula
shell
size
increases
as
a
function
of
time ;
the
sex
of
an
individual

is
correlated
with
its
size .
Males
are
often
found
stacked
on
top
of
females
-
this
is
the

position
necessary
for
copulation
( Charnov
1982 ) .
Hobday
( 1997 )
studied
the
movement
of

Crepidula
based
on
reproductive
potentials ,
hypothesizing
that
social
situation
can
affect
the

time
of
male - female
transition .
That
is ,
if
a
male
is
in
the
presence
of
females ,
it
may

change
to
a
female
later
than
if
it
were
alone ,
in
order
to
maximize
its
reproductive
potential .

This
means
that
the
sex
of
a
Crepidula
cannot
be
determined
solely
by
its
size .
Later
in
this

paper
a
precise
way
of
determining
the
sex
of
a
Crepidula
will
be
explained
in
further
detail .

Crepidula
are
filter
feeders
and
can
live
in
a
sedentary
state
indefinitely .
Vermeij
et

al .
( 1987 )
studied
the
interaction
between
Crepidula
adunca
on
the
host
snail
Calliostoma

ligatum
and
showed
that
Crepidula
who
had
been
moved
from
their
host
shell
and

reattached
were
more
likely
to
be
attacked
by
predators
since
they
no
longer
had
as
close
a

fit .
Crepidula
shell
size
increases
as
a
function
of
time .
Therefore
the
fit
of
a
Crepidula
on

a
host
improves
with
time .
Movement
therefore
makes
them
more
vulnerable
to
predators
